title: DATASUCKERS vs the ATB retail chain: a 10-step attack
summary: According to the DATASUCKERS group, the ATB retail chain was not broken through a single hole but through a chain of ten small steps. Each looked minor; together they gave access to databases, mail and source code. The breakdown shows which class of solution could stop the attack, or reduce the damage, at each step.
body: This is a retelling of an incident breakdown by Alesta (a 15-slide deck marked for partners). It is written in plain language for people who do not work in security every day. It has little technical detail: no vulnerability numbers (CVEs), tool names, versions or indicators of compromise.

The deck's main idea is that the chain breaks at any link. First, passwords turned up in public view, then came an injection into a database query and open registration on a portal. After that, reading internal files, a web shell, a reused password and a master key inside a backup. All of this, per the group's claim, happened in one evening.

Below, each step is described the way the deck presents it, with an everyday analogy. Next to each step are the classes of solutions that stop or compensate it, and an explanation of how. The deck itself does not map steps to MITRE ATT&CK techniques: that is CyberPlain's editorial tagging, marked with an asterisk.

All figures and facts of the attack come from the group's claims and partial confirmations by companies. We have not verified them and make no verdict on what exactly happened. The wording "per the group's claim" applies to every step.

claims.label: customers whose data was allegedly stolen

claimsNote: All figures are claims by the group and partial confirmations by companies; not independently verified.

actor.name: DATASUCKERS
profile: A financially motivated group: as the deck describes it, it steals data and demands money for non-disclosure, or sells the data.
Communicates in Russian and publishes leaks and threats on Telegram.

Targets large B2C companies with large personal-data sets. The deck also lists other claims by the group: Tez Tour (September 2026) and Dodo Pizza (about 29 September 2026). These are claims too, not independently confirmed.

steps.title: Secrets lying in plain sight
steps.what: According to the group's claim, the attacker unpacked the mobile app and found passwords written directly into the code. A separate service page with no password returned configuration that included database and mail passwords. It is like leaving spare keys under the doormat and hanging a sign on the door.

solutions.why: Shows the external perimeter as the attacker sees it, including forgotten public pages. The service page without a password could have been spotted and closed before the attack.

Scans sites and services and finds exposed configuration and common vulnerabilities. In the deck this role is played by Check Point Threat Exposure Management, which is not in the site's portfolio, so we show the closest class.
Keeps passwords in a vault with rotation instead of in code or configuration files. Even if a password leaks, it quickly stops working.
Removes passwords written into code: the app receives them from a vault at run time. The deck does not name this separately; it is an editorial addition.

gaps: Finding passwords in code before release (SAST) — the deck names it as the main tool here. CyberPlain has no separate class for it.

steps.title: SQL injection on the main site
steps.what: According to the group's claim, through an ordinary filter field on the site the attacker made the database return other people's data. The deck mentions about 8 million customers with phones and emails (the headline says 7.9 million; both figures are from the deck). An analogy: one more request was slipped into the order window, and the cashier carried it out.
tools: SQL injection in a filter field

solutions.why: Sits in front of the site and recognises requests with an injection in the filter field. Such a request is blocked before it reaches the database.
Tests the running site from the outside and finds the field that allows injection. The hole can be fixed before an attacker uses it.
Simulates such requests against your defences and shows whether the WAF really stops them. The deck lists BAS for this step in its summary table.

gaps: Finding vulnerabilities in code before release (SAST) — the deck names it as the root-cause fix. CyberPlain has no separate class for it.

steps.title: Self-registration on the supplier portal
steps.what: According to the group's claim, the partner portal let anyone register without checks or moderation. The attacker created a legitimate account and got inside. It is like an office door that opens for anyone who calls themselves a supplier.

solutions.why: Requires a second factor at sign-in, portals included. A newly created account without confirmation does not get in so easily. In the deck this role is played by Silverfort Identity Protection.
Watches who signs in, from where and to what, and notices an unusual sign-in by a new account. It lets you block it or ask for an extra check.

Finds risky settings, such as open registration or weak moderation, before someone uses them. In the deck this is Check Point Threat Exposure Management, which is not in the site's portfolio, so we show the closest class.

gaps: Registration moderation on the portal is a setting of the application itself, not a separate class of solution. The portal owner needs to check it and turn it on.

steps.title: Reading other people's files on the server
steps.what: According to the group's claim, through the portal the attacker made the server show internal system files (local file inclusion, LFI). In one of them, passwords for three production databases lay in clear text. It is like asking a librarian to look in someone else's cabinet and read it aloud.

solutions.why: Recognises and blocks attempts to read system files through a portal request. The attacker never reaches the file's contents.
If database passwords are kept in a vault rather than in clear text in a file, the file that was read opens nothing. The attacker does not see a live password.

The app takes database passwords from a secrets vault at run time, so they are not in configuration files. Even if the file is read, there is nothing in it. The deck does not name this separately; it is an editorial addition.

gaps: Finding the file-read flaw in code (SAST) — the deck names it as the root-cause fix. CyberPlain has no separate class for it.

steps.title: Web shell and WAF bypass
steps.what: According to the group's claim, the attacker uploaded a disguised file that let him run commands on the server (a web shell). He got past the WAF by hiding the payload behind a large block of junk. The deck explains that inspecting the whole request body removes this trick. An analogy: a guard checks only the first page of a thick folder.
tools: junk block to bypass the WAF

solutions.why: Sees the web server suddenly start running commands, which it does not do normally, and stops it even after the WAF is bypassed. The deck calls this the "main stop" of the step.
A correctly configured WAF inspects the whole request body, so hiding the payload behind junk does not work.
Checks in advance whether your WAF really catches such bypasses, so the settings can be fixed before a real attack.

steps.title: Privilege escalation through the monitoring system
steps.what: According to the group's claim, the attacker signed in to the monitoring system with a stolen password, the same one used for mail. The system ran with top privileges, so he became an administrator. An analogy: the key to the break room turned out to be a master key to the whole building.

solutions.why: Notices a sign-in to a foreign system and signs of "one password everywhere", and can demand an extra check or block the sign-in. In the deck this is Silverfort Identity Protection.
A second factor means one stolen password is not enough to sign in to the monitoring system. Reusing the mail password no longer opens the door by itself.
Isolates administrative access, makes passwords unique and keeps sessions supervised. One password no longer opens several systems.

Shows that the monitoring system runs with excessive privileges and flags it as a critical risk. In the deck this is done by Check Point Threat Exposure Management, which is not in the site's portfolio, so we show the closest class.

steps.title: "Keys to everything" from backups
steps.what: According to the group's claim, through internal channels the attacker reached the backups. Inside lay the administrator's master SSH key, one key that opens all the network's servers at once. It is like keeping the master key in a safe with its own key lying next to it.
tools: master SSH key from a backup

solutions.why: Keys are kept not in backups but in a vault with rotation. One key does not open the whole network, and access to servers is issued under control and recorded.
Records the attacker moving between servers and the use of the stolen key. Movement across the network becomes visible.
Gathers events from different systems into one picture and signals unusual movement across the network. In the deck this is Rapid7 Incident Command.
Compares account behaviour with the norm and notices that an admin key is suddenly used at an unusual time or from unusual places.

steps.title: Access to all databases
steps.what: According to the group's claim, with stolen passwords the attacker connected to all the databases: customers and employees, including passport data. In one place the password was a default: admin / changeme. It is like leaving the factory code on a safe.

solutions.why: Finds default and weak passwords before an attacker does. In the deck this role is played by Check Point Threat Exposure Management, which is not in the site's portfolio, so we show the closest class.
Removes default and shared passwords and makes them unique and managed. The password admin / changeme stops working.
Sees mass "pulling" of databases as a deviation from the norm. The alarm fires while the data has not yet left. In the deck this is Rapid7 Incident Command.
Notices that an account reads databases in volumes and at times unusual for it, and raises an alarm.

steps.title: Access to corporate mail
steps.what: According to the group's claim, another stolen password opened corporate mail. The attacker exported thousands of emails, including live password-reset links for other systems. An analogy: someone else's mailbox holds spare keys to the neighbouring doors.

solutions.why: Requires a second factor to sign in to mail. A stolen password alone no longer opens the mailbox.
Also covers the "old" mail protocols, which usually have no MFA, a typical blind spot. In the deck this is Silverfort Identity Protection.
If the mailbox is a service one, access to it is controlled and recorded, and its password is not kept in clear text.

steps.title: Theft of all source code
steps.what: According to the group's claim, with the master key the attacker downloaded all of the company's source code, 524 projects. He also found an analytics system with a default password. It is like carrying the whole archive out of the office because the key fitted every cabinet.
tools: analytics system with a default password

solutions.why: Access to repositories goes through a controlled vault, not one key to everything. Mass copying of code without permission does not happen.
Sees mass copying and archiving of code on the server. That is a sign of theft which can be stopped on the spot.

Finds the default password in the analytics system (the same admin / changeme). In the deck this is done by Check Point Threat Exposure Management, which is not in the site's portfolio, so we show the closest class.

lessons: No single box saves you; the combination does. That is how the deck sums up the story (slide 15).
Before the attack: check the external perimeter and risky settings, to remove the open doors at the entrance.
During the attack: a WAF, EDR and account protection stop the attacker in motion.
Throughout: managing secrets and keys (PAM) breaks the chain in most places, because a stolen password no longer opens the whole network.
caveats: All figures and facts are claims by the group and partial confirmations by companies. The deck itself says they are not independently verified.
The deck has no CVE numbers, tool names, versions, commands or indicators of compromise. The mapping to ATT&CK techniques is editorial; it is not from the source.
The author and exact date of the deck are not stated. The products and vendors in it are the publisher's (Alesta) commercial position, not neutral analysis.
There are small discrepancies between slides: the summary matrix and the individual step slides do not fully agree on which product applies to which steps. We relied on the step slides.
